title.narrative: Supporting Enhancing Coordination Systems for Disaster Response in Nigeria (ECODiN) Program

description.narrative: Since the announcement of the Aid Cut in January 2025, there has been increase in vulnerabilities as bandit attacks intensify in Sokoto, Zamfara and Katsina States with more communities being displaced. Ongoing conflict have led to an acute protection crisis, displacing millions, destroying critical infrastructure, and disrupting livelihoods. This is worsened by the inability of shelters and host communities to cater for the needs of new arrivals in displacement camps. Due to the decrease in humanitarian services which has been largely funded by the BHA, there has been rise in protection concerns with young women and girls resorting to negative coping mechanisms to survive, with more households exposed to risks while trying to access livelihood opportunities to cater for basic household and shelter needs. This is compounded by limited access to water supply and increased cases of WaSH related diseases experienced by temporary shelters and host communities. In all of these, the institutions charged with coordinating response to immediate needs arising from climate and human-induced disasters are overwhelmed as Katsina still hosts the largest share of IDPs in North-West Nigeria followed by Zamfara State. Furthermore, the cuts have equally undermined the ability of humanitarian organizations and government agencies to effectively respond to emerging needs and support them to strengthen response and coordination mechanism in the states. Climate change, rapid population growth—projected to reach 400 million by 2050 according to the World Bank still pose high level threats as Nigeria remains one of Africa's most flood-prone countries. In the past year alone, flooding claimed 320 lives, affected 1.4 million people, displaced 730,000 individuals, destroyed 120,000 houses, and destroyed about 260,000 hectares of farmland resulting in harvest loss equivalent to food for 13 million people, thereby worsening food insecurity and causing waterborne disease. Without funding, this seismic shift may undo hard-won gains in the humanitarian landscape.
